h1: Landscaping and yard care in Esquimalt
summary: Esquimalt is compact and close to the water, from older homes near Saxe Point and West Bay to stratas in the village and lots on the Gorge. Its Natural Environment permit area covers much new landscaping and asks for mostly native plants chosen for wind and sea spray.

Trees are protected in the Township from 30 cm across, and arbutus, Garry oak and Pacific dogwood from just 4 cm. Along the Gorge, the first 7.5 m from the high-water mark is kept as natural as possible, and new buildings stay 20 m back.

localRules.text: Esquimalt's Tree Protection Bylaw, 2022, 3076 protects any tree 30 cm or more in diameter at breast height (1.4 m). It also protects native Douglas-fir, grand fir and western redcedar once 4 m tall, and arbutus, bigleaf maple, Garry oak, Pacific dogwood and Pacific yew from 4 cm DBH. Trees on steep slopes, wildlife and nest trees, and replacement trees are protected too.
localRules.excerpt: any tree regardless of species having a DBH of 30 centimetres or more

localRules.text: In Esquimalt you need a permit to cut, remove or alter a protected tree, even one that is dead, dying or hazardous. The permit form covers removal, pruning and work in the protected root zone, and applications go to trees@esquimalt.ca.
localRules.sourceTitle: Trees & Urban Forestry | Township of Esquimalt
localRules.excerpt: You will need a permit to cut, remove or alter a protected tree. This includes trees which are dead, dying, or hazardous.

localRules.text: Esquimalt residents may prune overhanging branches under 4 inches (about 10 cm) in diameter from a neighbour's tree, following ISA practice. Larger limbs need a tree cutting permit.
localRules.sourceTitle: Trees & Urban Forestry | Township of Esquimalt
localRules.excerpt: Residents are within their rights to prune overhanging branches that are less than 4 inches in diameter from neighbouring trees.

localRules.text: Esquimalt's Natural Environment Development Permit Area (DPA 1) covers new buildings and structures, additions over 10 m² and landscaping, with some exceptions. Township-approved ecological restoration and new permeable paths under 1 m wide are exempt.
localRules.excerpt: This Development Permit Area applies to: New buildings and structures … Landscaping (with some exceptions)

localRules.text: Within Esquimalt's DPA 1, new development is not permitted within 20 m of the high-water mark of the Gorge Waterway, or within 10 m of the high-water mark of the Strait of Juan de Fuca.
localRules.excerpt: Within Development Permit Area No 1 – Natural Environment, new development is not permitted: within 20 metres of the high water mark of the Gorge Waterway

localRules.text: Esquimalt's DPA 1 guidelines ask that land within 7.5 m of the Gorge Waterway's high-water mark be kept as natural as possible, and restored with native trees and plants where it has been altered.
localRules.sourceTitle: DPA 1: Natural Environment guidelines (Township of Esquimalt)
localRules.excerpt: Land within 7.5m of the high watermark of the Gorge Waterway shall be retained in as natural a state as possible.

localRules.text: Esquimalt's DPA 1 guidelines ask designers to avoid disturbing or compacting natural soil, to frame public views rather than block them, to prefer natural topography over blasting or retaining walls, and to aim to meet the Canadian Landscape Standards.
localRules.sourceTitle: DPA 1: Natural Environment guidelines (Township of Esquimalt)
localRules.excerpt: Avoid disturbing, compacting and removing areas of natural soil

localRules.text: Esquimalt's DPA 1 guidelines say new landscaping should be mostly native plants and trees, preferably Coastal Douglas-fir zone species, with 'nature out front' in front yards. Plants should be chosen for site conditions, including wind exposure and sea-spray tolerance.
localRules.sourceTitle: DPA 1: Natural Environment guidelines (Township of Esquimalt)
localRules.excerpt: New landscaping shall consist predominantly of native plant and tree species.

localRules.text: Esquimalt's Pesticide Use Reduction Bylaw 2686 regulates and reduces non-essential (cosmetic) pesticide use on lawns, trees, shrubs and flowers on residential and public property. It applies to landscape professionals and lawn care companies as well as residents. Reduced-risk pesticides on the bylaw's list are allowed, and other use needs a permit as a last resort.
localRules.sourceTitle: Important Notice to Home Owners, Tenants, Gardeners and Landscapers regarding the use of Pesticides (Township of Esquimalt)
localRules.excerpt: applies to all Esquimalt property owners and residents as well as landscape professionals and lawn care companies that do business within the Township of Esquimalt

localRules.text: Under Esquimalt's Boulevard Maintenance Bylaw 2860, changing a boulevard needs a Boulevard Alteration Permit. Boulevard shrubs must be drought tolerant and kept under 0.5 m, rocks and gravel need a permit, grass is kept at 15 cm or less, and noxious or invasive plants are not allowed.
localRules.sourceTitle: Boulevard Maintenance Bylaw 2860, consolidated July 2019 (Township of Esquimalt)
localRules.excerpt: noxious weeds or invasive plants are not permitted

conditions.text: Esquimalt holds one of Victoria Harbour's last Garry oak sites, the 2.4-acre Matson Conservation Area run by a local land trust, according to the trust's own page. Gardens nearby suit native, invasive-free planting.

proof.text: Moved a West Bay strata's shrub beds from spray heads to drip and left the boulevard strip in grass kept under the Township's 15 cm limit.

servicesBlurb.grounds-maintenance: Older Esquimalt lots with mature hedges and small lawns need steady care, and lawn-care companies working there follow the Township's pesticide bylaw too.
servicesBlurb.landscape-installation: New planting inside DPA 1 leans on Coastal Douglas-fir zone natives and 'nature out front' in the front yard.
servicesBlurb.irrigation: Converting spray heads to drip suits the Township's small beds and its drought-tolerant boulevard shrubs, which the bylaw keeps under 0.5 m.
servicesBlurb.tree-vegetation: Neighbours may prune overhanging branches under about 10 cm in Esquimalt, while larger limbs and any protected tree need a Township permit.
